profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a SaaS company building an AI-based support-ticket triage feature for its customer support platform. After reviewing findings from recent RE4AI literature on requirements specification, explainability, and the gap between ML engineers and end-users, the team wants to define a lightweight but repeatable requirements process before starting a limited production pilot. The agenda is to agree on what artifacts need to be produced, what the pilot includes, who owns each preparation task, and what must happen before sign-off. The expected outcome is a shared plan for the next two weeks covering the feature spec, evaluation and explainability materials, pilot readiness tasks, and review timing.

members.name: Nina Rao
members.expertise: Backend delivery, cross-functional execution, production rollout planning for customer support systems
members.background: Nina started as a product analyst, moved into backend engineering, and now manages the team responsible for the support agent workspace and routing services.
members.private_state: She wants to keep the AI initiative within the quarter's committed delivery window, avoid adding heavyweight documentation that could slow implementation, and prevent the pilot from expanding into a riskier launch than leadership expects.
hidden_assumptions: When a team says the 'spec' is done, that usually means the product requirements doc, API notes, and Jira acceptance criteria are complete; governance-oriented AI artifacts can be added later if needed.
A 'pilot in support' naturally means a narrow agent-facing trial in the North America enterprise queue, not backend behavior that changes live routing outcomes.
If the UI gives agents a short reason snippet for a suggestion, the explainability requirement is effectively covered for this phase.
The 'golden set' is the March manually reviewed sample of 500 enterprise tickets that operations has already been using for sanity checks.

members.name: Leo Martins
members.role: ML Tech Lead, Applied AI Platform
members.expertise: NLP systems, model evaluation, MLOps, AI governance and deployment readiness
members.background: Leo leads the applied ML group that builds internal language models and inference services, and previously worked on high-stakes ML review processes in a regulated health-tech environment.
members.private_state: He wants enough upfront requirements detail to avoid late-stage compliance and trust issues, and he sees this project as a chance to establish a reusable RE pattern for future AI features across the company.
hidden_assumptions: For an AI feature, the 'spec' includes intended behavior boundaries, fallback rules, data assumptions, monitoring expectations, and inputs needed for the model card and risk review.

A 'pilot in support' should exercise the actual production service path for one queue, including background tagging or routing recommendations, otherwise it does not test the real operational behavior.

Explainability is only truly covered when there is an internal rationale package with data provenance, limitation statements, and traceable evidence for reviewers, even if end-users see only a simple summary.
The 'golden set' is the benchmark suite in the ML evaluation repository from Q4, which includes multilingual slices and curated edge cases used for release checks.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk about 'getting the spec done' before implementation starts.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a conventional delivery spec: PRD updates, service/API notes, and acceptance criteria sufficient for sprint execution.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means an AI requirements package that also includes behavior boundaries, fallback conditions, explainability expectations, and governance inputs.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both work in engineering organizations where 'spec' is a routine planning term, so it feels too familiar to unpack; each assumes the other shares the local default for what a finished spec contains.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the 'pilot in support'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to run a 'pilot in support for the enterprise queue.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means an agent-assist pilot limited to the visible suggestion panel for North America enterprise agents, with existing manual tagging and routing unchanged.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the full model-backed service path is active for that queue, including automatic pre-tagging or routing recommendations behind the scenes, with human override available.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see 'pilot' as a restricted rollout and treat the boundary between UI exposure and backend operational effects as an implementation detail rather than a planning item worth re-stating.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means for explainability to be 'covered'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they need to make sure 'explainability is covered' in the requirements.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks explainability is covered if the agent UI shows a short reason phrase such as top factors or a confidence cue, enough for support staff to trust the suggestion.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks explainability is covered only if there is an internal review package documenting rationale traces, data provenance, limitations, and evidence suitable for approval and later audits.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Explainability is already accepted as important for AI systems, so the phrase signals strong alignment at a high level; neither feels a need to define the completion standard because each assumes their notion is the obvious one.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to validating the feature against 'the golden set' before sign-off.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the March 500-ticket manually reviewed operations sample currently used by the support platform team for sanity checks.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the Q4 benchmark suite in the ML repo that contains curated edge cases, multilingual tickets, and evaluation slices used by the ML team.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Each believes there is already one canonical benchmark everyone informally knows about, so the definite phrase 'the golden set' creates a false sense of shared reference.

turns.inner_thought: I want this to stay very practical. We already got useful takeaways from the RE4AI readout, but I do not want that turning into a big-process exercise. If we can get the spec done by next Wednesday with the PRD updates, service notes, and Jira acceptance criteria, the team can start implementation without jeopardizing the quarter. Any extra AI governance docs can follow if someone really needs them before launch.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. The main goal today is to turn the RE4AI lessons into a concrete two-week plan and get the spec done by next Wednesday so the pilot stays on the quarter timeline. I'd like us to leave with clear owners for the prep work and a clean path to sign-off.

turns.inner_thought: Good, but if we're saying the spec is done next Wednesday, it has to include the actual AI requirements package, not just build tickets. I need behavior boundaries, fallback expectations, monitoring assumptions, and the pieces that feed the model card and review. And if explainability is covered, that has to mean enough material for internal reviewers, not just something visible in the product.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. From my side, getting the spec done should include the decision boundaries, fallback behavior, and the explainability pieces we'll need before we move forward. If we line that up now, the rest of the prep should be much smoother.

turns.inner_thought: I want to keep the rollout narrow: agent-assist only, North America enterprise queue, no changes to live routing behavior. Calling it a pilot in support for the enterprise queue should already imply that. I mostly need to know what ML dependencies there are so platform can plan the workspace integration and rollout checklist.
turns.utterance: Agreed. In terms of scope, I think we start with a pilot in support for the enterprise queue first. What does your team need to have in place to make that happen on your side?

turns.inner_thought: For this to be a meaningful pilot in support for the enterprise queue, we need the model running on the actual production path for that queue. I want override controls and shadow logging immediately so we can observe behavior safely while still exercising the real service. Otherwise we'll learn very little about operational drift or trust issues.
turns.utterance: We can support that. My team can wire the model into the enterprise queue path, put override controls around it, and set up shadow logging during the first week of the pilot. That would give us enough signal to evaluate behavior without losing control.

turns.inner_thought: I need to head off anything too heavy here. Explainability is covered for this phase if agents get a short reason snippet in the workspace so the suggestions don't feel opaque. That's enough for trust in a limited rollout, and it shouldn't slow engineering down with a huge artifact backlog.
turns.utterance: That sounds workable. One thing I'd like to keep lightweight this round is explainability. If we make sure explainability is covered in a simple way in the workspace, I think we can support the pilot without slowing the rollout.

turns.inner_thought: I'm fine with a simple experience for agents, but I need the internal package too. Explainability is only covered if the review materials document provenance, limitations, rationale support, and evidence for approval. This is exactly the kind of project where we should set the pattern correctly, even if the external presentation stays light.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's fine with me as long as explainability is covered in the review materials too. We should include the limitations and supporting evidence needed for approval, and then keep the user-facing part as streamlined as we want.

turns.inner_thought: Before sign-off, QA can run the March 500-ticket manually reviewed sample that ops already trusts, and then ops can sanity-check a handful of fresh enterprise tickets. That's plenty for a narrow pilot. No need to invent another benchmark path when we already have the golden set everyone uses on the support side.
turns.utterance: On validation, I think QA can run the feature against the golden set before sign-off, and then operations can spot-check a few recent enterprise tickets just to make sure we're comfortable with what comes back.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. We'll rerun the Q4 benchmark suite from the ML repo after threshold tuning, especially the multilingual and edge-case slices, and include those results in the readiness packet. That's the golden set we use for release checks, so it should satisfy the evidence bar cleanly.
turns.utterance: Works for me. My team will rerun the golden set after threshold tuning and attach the slice-level results to the readiness packet so we have something concrete for the review.

turns.inner_thought: Okay, this sounds contained enough if I keep us moving. I'll drive the conventional build spec and launch checklist; Leo can bring whatever evaluation and review docs his team wants, as long as it doesn't block engineering. The pilot in support for the enterprise queue still sounds like the narrow agent-facing trial I need, and if explainability is covered we should be safe for this quarter.
turns.utterance: Let me summarize the split, then. I'll finish the spec and the launch checklist from the platform side, and you'll handle the evaluation work and the review materials for the pilot. If we both keep moving in parallel, we should be in good shape by next week.

turns.inner_thought: That division works. I want a Monday draft review so I can verify the spec actually includes the AI boundaries and approval inputs, and once the golden set results are in, we should have enough to push through sign-off. This could become a reusable template if we capture it cleanly.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. Why don't we do a draft review on Monday? If the spec is in decent shape by then and the golden-set results are lined up right after, I think we'll be ready for pilot sign-off.
